claims.text: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a 5–10 nm molybdenum layer before copper infiltration will create an engineered, coherent W–Mo–Cu interface.
The engineered W–Mo–Cu interface will minimize interfacial thermal resistance.
The Mo coating will significantly increase the bulk thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The Mo-coated composite will preserve mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
SPS consolidation at 800–900 °C under an inert atmosphere can provide suitable densification while maintaining the thin Mo layer without excessive diffusion.
The W–Mo–Cu interface reduces interfacial scattering of electrons and phonons.
The ultrathin Mo layer improves atomic bonding between tungsten and copper by reducing interfacial mismatches.
Improved interfacial bonding lowers thermal boundary resistance and enables more efficient heat flow through the composite.
The interface modification maintains the inherent mechanical and irradiation properties of tungsten and copper.
Relative to an uncoated W–Cu composite, the Mo-coated composite will have measurably higher bulk thermal conductivity.
Relative to an uncoated W–Cu composite, the Mo-coated composite will have comparable or improved mechanical strength.
Relative to an uncoated W–Cu composite, the Mo-coated composite will have comparable or improved irradiation resilience.
Processing outside 800–900 °C or prolonged thermal cycling or irradiation may cause Mo-layer diffusion and loss of interfacial integrity.
The long-term stability of the Mo layer under extended high-temperature and irradiation exposure is uncertain.
